name: oe-kimi-F-S-P
finalResponse:
The brief says "produce a turnaround-or-exit assessment," which usually means a deck with two columns and a recommendation disguised as a finding. What follows is more like a reading of the evidence — much of it already provided by the unit itself, which has been answering the question for three years. Loosely held, because the market will grade the homework.

**The restructurings were the experiment; the results are in.** Two rounds of cost cuts that did not touch the losses tell you the problem was never the cost base. Execution problems yield to sharp knives; this one didn't. So look at structure: price realization against the best competitor, utilization, the shape of demand in each served niche. The cleanest test is unglamorous — if the best-run rival in this space earns a real margin, the gap is closable and the diagnosis is execution. If the best rival is also treading water, the structure itself is the verdict. One caution: three bad years leave scar tissue that mimics structural decline. The diagnosis must separate the market's opinion from the organization's exhaustion. *Is the house cold, or have we just stopped lighting fires?*

**The managers have already voted.** Talent transferring out is the most honest data in the building — an internal exit poll, more reliable than any engagement survey. Note where they went. People flee toward value, and their destinations map where in this group the future is believed to live. Any plan that does not first stop this flow is rearranging furniture. Retention here costs less than replacement, and it buys the one thing a one-year clock cannot manufacture: people who know where the contracts are buried.

**Ask the customers who buy twice.** The shared customers are the Rosetta stone. They buy profitably from the group and services from this unit — one might ask why they keep both relationships. Either the service is genuinely valued, in which case there is a right to win, or it is procurement inertia, in which case it evaporates the moment anyone leans on it. Do not ask them about satisfaction. Ask what they would do if the unit closed. *Who would call to complain — and who would simply call a competitor?*

**Build the P&L the unit actually has.** Not the allocated one — the true one, contract by contract, with real cost-to-serve. Industrial services almost always decomposes the same way: long-term maintenance and framework agreements that behave like annuities; project work won in auctions, where the winner's curse does the accounting; and emergency call-out work, high-margin and reputation-driven. Expect to find the losses concentrated in the bid-driven middle, where the unit is subscale, and the profit hiding in the sticky, unglamorous agreements where response time and trust outrank price. The turnaround, if there is one, is a shrink-to-core: keep the annuities, leave the auctions.

**Write the year as four gates, not twelve months.** The board said a year; hear it as four questions, each with a pre-agreed answer.

- *Gate 1, day 90:* diagnosis signed, loss-making contracts named, key people locked, no new bids below a margin floor. The tell: attrition stops.
- *Gate 2, month 6:* portfolio pruned, bad contracts renegotiated or exited, breakeven run-rate visible on the remaining core.
- *Gate 3, month 9:* the core is growing — order-book coverage above one in retained segments, a customer renewing early, the first evidence of pricing power.
- *Gate 4, month 12:* a trailing quarter at or near breakeven with line of sight to target margin — or the trigger fires.

A milestone that can be renegotiated at month eleven is a hope wearing a date. Set the kill criteria now, in writing, while they are still cheap to honor.

**Decide the exit before you need it.** Sketch the alternatives while there is still something to sell, because the same work that finds the profitable core is the work that makes the unit sellable. A trade sale to a consolidator, who buys route density and contracts you cannot monetize. A sale to a competitor, who may pay most for the order book and the people you cannot keep. A management buyout — the managers who haven't left yet might purchase what the group cannot run, on generous terms and a clean perimeter. Or the quietest option, often the richest: fold the profitable sliver into a healthy division and wind down the rest, keeping twenty percent of the revenue and none of the structure. Straight run-off is the last resort; contracts and people make it slower and costlier than the spreadsheet suggests. And note what the shared customers complicate: a sloppy exit sells the crown-jewel relationships along with the unit. The perimeter of the deal matters more than the headline price. *What is the buyer actually buying — and what are we accidentally selling?*

**Choose with criteria, not courage.** The decision between turnaround and divestment, made now rather than at the deadline: Is there a defensible niche, evidenced by someone earning a structural margin in it? Can the core reach breakeven run-rate within the year for an investment smaller than the cost of exit? And the full accounting — stranded costs, severance, contract penalties, and the quiet tax that a bleeding unit levies on the attention of the profitable divisions. The board's one-year clock, viewed correctly, is not the constraint. It is the gift: the forcing function for a question that three years of patience avoided. *What would we do if we weren't allowed to wait?*

**Watch the tell, not the pack.** The board deck will want milestones. Count instead the transfer requests. If the best people stop trying to leave, the turnaround is working before the P&L admits it. If the flow accelerates, the market inside the building has already graded the homework.

One thing worth sitting with: turnaround and exit are not two plans. They are one plan with a deadline — the disciplined search for the profitable core either produces a business worth keeping or an asset worth buying, and you cannot know which until you do the work. A business, like a brand, is a promise. The only question is whether anyone still needs it kept — and the answer, here as elsewhere, belongs to the customer, not the committee.
